Beyond its dangers as an individuated practice, white racial contempt reflects wider patterns of social formation and habits of epistemic deference. To explore these dynamics, the power of active and culpable ignorance is examined through an analysis of epistemologies of resistance. Focusing on resistant forms of racial ignorance permits (1) a robust sense of the interplay between self and social knowledge, (2) a fluid conception of testimonial and hermeneutical injustice, and (3) a dynamic and interactive account of epistemic responsibility. The constructive sections of the chapter explore how racial contempt often emerges in (1) the narration of space, (2) the experience of racial soundscapes, (3) the disavowal of opacity in the interior and social lives of black people, and (4) the politics of self-trust and social suspicion. This chapter shows how viewing racial contempt as an outgrowth of misplaced deference can enrich repertoires of resistance, conceptually and practically.
